proves: a border is the ring between the border box and the padding box, inside the box, with both rings rounded
cases: box 1: uniform 4px border, 12px radius - one ring fill, no clip
box 2: widths top 2 right 8 bottom 5 left 0, radii tl 20 tr 0 br 10 bl 4, one edge taking border_color_all
box 3: 24px radius against widths differing five to one, so the arcs and the corner transitions are unmissable
checkable: the border is INSIDE the box. Box 1's 4px border spans x 8..127 of a box at 8..127; a stroke centred on the box edge would span 6..129 and hang half outside, which is what this pinned before.
also-checkable: box 2's red top edge starts at y=21 at its left end and y=20 at its right, following the 20px top-left arc. A border ignoring the radius is flat at one y across the whole width.
specification: CSS Backgrounds 3 5.2 for the inner radii (each axis reduced by that side's width, floored at zero) and 4.4 for the corner transition (a straight line from the outer corner point to the inner corner point, so unequal widths move the join without it being computed)
status: target, not a limitation: a square corner stays square, a rounded one follows its radius, a stroke sits inside the box rather than straddling its edge, and each corner's arc is divided where CSS Backgrounds 3 4.4 divides it - measured in Chrome, not inferred from this picture.
checkable-vertically: a row reads the left and right edges and no other, so each box is read down a column as well: at x=60 box 1 is border 20-23, fill 24-95, border 96-99, which is its 4 top and bottom; at x=190 box 2 is red 20-21 (its 2 top), fill 22-94, grey 95-99 (its 5 bottom); at x=320 box 3 is red 20-29, fill 30-89, blue 90-99. The widths differ per edge, so a bottom edge drawn as anything but a bar of exactly that thickness shows here and in no row sample. `borders-square` is why this field exists: it named rows only, and a diagonal bottom edge passed it for a day.
corner-transitions-are-chrome's: the two rounded corners in this fixture are pinned against Chrome rather than against this image, by crates/meo-canvas-core/tests/chrome_corner_truth.rs. Chrome's numbers, read from its own painted bytes via an SVG foreignObject into a canvas and getImageData (scratchpad/chrome/corner-truth.tsv): box 2's top-left, with a zero-width left edge, is RED at the outer boundary for every row of the arc, y=0 to 18 from the box's top, then the box's own fill from y=19 where the radius ends, and BLUE at no row at all. Box 3's top-left, 10px top against 2px left, is red to y=12, a red-and-yellow blend at y=13, and yellow from y=14.
why-that-is-a-separate-file: this fixture certified both of those corners while they were wrong, twice, because it was accepted from our own render. It says 'this is the picture'; only a browser says 'this is the right picture'. The handover row is the discriminator and no golden can hold it: closing a gap in the ring does not put the join where CSS puts it, and a ring drawn in one colour cannot show the join at all.
what-moved-and-why: boxes 2 and 3 both changed when the corner division was fixed. Each edge had been clipped to the quadrilateral outer corner, outer corner, inner corner, inner corner, which is the right region only where the corner is square: where it is rounded the ring sweeps past the inner box's own edge into a part of the corner that quadrilateral does not contain. Box 2 lost most of its top-left arc to an edge of zero width; box 3 showed its own background at x=268..272, y=30..38 of this image. Box 1, uniform 4px, is the only cell here that did not move - and a uniform cell cannot see a division error at all, since both sides of every join are the same width and the same colour.
